citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
At the time of the inspection, the facility did not have a Program of Veterinary Care from their new Attending Veterinarian
(AV). The AV is part-time. The facility stated they have a site visit scheduled with their new AV for October 7, 2026.
A written program of veterinary care is required to address the requirements for adequate veterinary care. Regular visits
to the facility are important because the AV evaluates the animals and their care and can give important professional
advice regarding the health and welfare of the animals including all aspects of their husbandry.
Each dealer and exhibitor shall employ an attending veterinarian under formal arrangements. In the case of a part-time
attending veterinarian or consultant arrangements, the formal arrangements shall include a written program of veterinary
care and regularly scheduled visits to the premises of the dealer or exhibitor.

The facility failed to remove excessive excreta in an enclosure housing one domestic short-haired rabbit.
An excessive accumulation of feces was mixed throughout the litter. The litter was also discolored and stained yellow in
some areas indicating continued heavy urine accumulation. Excessive accumulations of feces can allow for the spread of
disease hazards, create unpleasant odors and attract pests.
Primary enclosures shall be kept reasonably free of excreta, hair, cobwebs and other debris by periodic cleaning.
Correct by October 5, 2026.

The facility failed to remove excreta from the wooly possums’ primary enclosures to prevent contamination of the animals
contained therein and to minimize disease hazards and to reduce odors.
The wooly possum’s enclosure has an excessive accumulation of excreta, fur and/or discarded food present in the catch
tray. The inspector observed fruit flies in and around the enclosure.
Accumulations of feces, urine, and soiled bedding are harmful to the animals as they can spread disease, attract pests,
and cause unpleasant odors. Excreta shall be removed from primary enclosures as often as necessary to prevent
contamination of the animals contained therein and to minimize disease hazards and to reduce odors.

The facility failed to keep the premises clean.
The outdoor backyard area had an assortment of unused crates, trash, and other discarded materials scattered
throughout the grass. The USDA inspector had to carefully maneuver around and move some of these obstacles to
evaluate the enclosures for the Spotted Genets and Coatimundis.
The carpet under the indoor primary enclosure for three chinchillas had an excessive accumulation of excreta, fur and/or
discarded food present. The inspector observed fruit flies around the enclosure.
Failure to adequately clean the premises can lead to illness, transmission of diseases, and attract unwanted pests. The
facility must ensure that the premises are kept clean and in good repair to protect the animals from injury to facilitate the
prescribed husbandry practices set forth in this subpart.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with a facility representative.
You may appeal all or part of any inspection report by submitting a written statement contesting the findings—along with
any supporting documentation—to the Deputy Administrator. Appeals of routine, focused, or attempted inspections must
be received within 21 days of report issuance as shown by the signature line of this report.
Appeals may be sent by email to AnimalCare@usda.gov.
Appeals sent by mail should be addressed to:
Deputy Administrator
APHIS Animal Care (AC)
U.S. Department of Agriculture
2150 Centre Avenue, Building B
Mailstop #3W11
Fort Collins, CO 80526-8117
